children: Ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, financial advisors broadly agree with the polling consensus that Democrats will retake the House of Representatives. But those we spoke to in recent days are split on whether Democrats can wrest the Senate away from Republicans as well. Either way, Democrats will have more power within a divided government, and that could favor certain stock market sectors. For this week's Barron's Advisor Big Q, we asked four wealth managers for their predictions on the election and how the outcome might impact markets.

Rami Sarafa, CEO, Cordoba Advisory Partners: There is a consensus that the Democrats are going to take the House for sure, and a pretty broad consensus now that they will win the Senate. They might even pick up seats in places that were deep red, like Kansas, Alaska, etc., which would be a big repudiation of Trump's agenda the past few years.

Polling has been notoriously bad in recent years, so I try not to put too much emphasis on that. But I do trust markets, and markets are pricing in a Democratic sweep. One sign is that interest rates on the long end have come down a little bit. That tells you that the market isn't pricing in runaway spending on the Iran war, which means investors think Democrats will rein in Trump to some degree. You're also seeing some frothiness within things like AI data centers, which means the market thinks some of this AI boom is going to stop. And that is very much a Democratic trade. Defense stocks have not done as well as they should in a year of war like this. That is another sign.

Then there's the question of what Democrats will do with their newfound power. There are a few themes we've been discussing and agree on internally. Medicaid and healthcare will be a big topic: Healthcare could see a boost because Medicaid cuts could be reversed. Some of Trump's executive orders to gut Obamacare and whatnot would be put on the back foot. The AI buildout, specifically data centers, has become a big issue. If Democrats sweep, that might hit this AI boom a bit. I don't think it will stop the momentum, because a lot of these things have very long tail lives and they're determined by state governments. I don't think it will end the AI party overnight. But it can definitely throw cold water on the boom.

Chris Grisanti, chief market strategist at MAI Capital Management: Everybody thinks, including me, that the Democrats will win the House easily. But I differ from the consensus that the Democrats will eke out a win in the Senate. I think the Republicans stand a good chance to hold the Senate. In the past several elections, anecdotally, it seems that the Republicans tend to do a little better than the polls predict. The Democrats could win Texas, and they could beat Susan Collins in Maine, and yes, a progressive could win in a swing state like Michigan, but it's hard to imagine all those things happening together. I just think it's going to be hard for them to run the table. I mean, they have to win several states that Trump won by at least 9%.

I would think there'll be a relief rally in the market if the Republicans hold the Senate. But that will be short-lived. The most important thing right now is what's happening with AI spending. I'm relatively optimistic on that: I think AI spending into 2027 looks very strong. The market's going through some angst right now, but this is just normal to me. I would expect the market to see capital spending plans as negative, but the earnings are going to be there, and that is the important thing. I think it will carry the market into 2027.

I think the impact of the election will be short term. Either it will be a nonevent because the Democrats will win both chambers marginally as expected, or there'll be a slight rally because the Republicans hold the Senate. But by the end of the year that won't be the headline.

Daniel Emerson, founder, private wealth advisor, Harbor View Private Wealth: Our base case is that one chamber will flip, and I think there's a pretty good chance both will. That to me is a best-case scenario. Historically markets do pretty well with a divided government, and [since Republicans will still control the executive branch], I think that we'll finally have some good checks and balances. Gridlock tends to be a good thing. When it comes to AI, which I think will continue to be an important theme, it could cause Democrats and Republicans to come together and actually pass legislation. That will hopefully take away some of the fearmongering around data center buildouts.

I like the midterms as a clearing event — an event removing uncertainty — in general. In each of the past 19 midterm years dating back to 1950, markets have been positive six months later, returning 14% on average. I think the midterms serving as a clearing event is a very predictable pattern, and it tells you that markets hate uncertainty even more than they might hate a known outcome. From a positioning standpoint, I like small caps in that environment. I like the technology trade. I like financials. Healthcare has a lot of momentum, so we're going to continue keeping exposure there. If I had to name my two favorite trades from here through the next six months, if midterms go the way I view them, they would probably be small caps and technology.

Matthew Liebman, founding partner and CEO, Amplius Wealth Advisors: My call is Democrats are going to take the House, but Republicans are going to hold the Senate. And I think it's going to be neutral to mildly positive for the market. It will remove legislative surprises.

Either nothing will get accomplished, which I think is reasonably market-friendly, or there is the off chance that both sides will create some sort of centrist compromise on some issues, which is also market-friendly. I think anything that avoids extremes in either direction is market-friendly, and I think that is what we're going to get. I do think with Democrats gaining more control they might try to put the tech industry in the crosshairs, but I don't see any major changes there legislatively. I think we'll see sort of more of the same, where earnings still drive the bus.
